Influences on Child Development 
Parents potentially influence their children in two entirely separate ways. First there is the effect 
of the genes: a biological parent shares with each child 50 per cent of his or her genes so parents 
obviously exert a genetic influence on the child. Second, in most families, there is the social or 
environmental influence on children of growing up in close proximity to their parents. 
 
Behavioural genetics attempts to estimate the relative contributions of genes and the environment 
by conducting studies on twins and other siblings. The results of such studies estimate that the 
environment accounts for between 50 and 60 per cent of the influence on their development. It 
therefore follows that genes account for 40–50 per cent of the influence. 
 
Behavioural geneticists further divide the environment into two separate forces: the shared 
environment, which consists of the influences common to all siblings and the unique or non-
shared environment, which consists of all the influences that are specific to an individual. These 
three effects – the genes, the shared environment and the unique environment – are considered to 
be the only effects on child development. 
 
The results of diverse pieces of research on the effect of the environment lead to the same 
conclusion: the shared environment accounts for few or none of the traits left over when you take 
out the genetic effects. One might think that identical twins reared in the same household would 
be more similar to each other than those reared apart; in fact there is very little difference between 
them (Plomin, Chipuer and Neiderhiser, 1994). Other research indicates that unrelated children 
who are adopted and brought up as siblings in the same family environment are no more similar 
to each other than any two unrelated children chosen at random from a population (Plomin and 
Daniels, 1987). At most, the data suggests that the shared environment accounts for 10 per cent of 
the similarities among siblings (Turkenheimer, 2000). 
 
If genes account for 50 per cent of the variation among people in general and the shared 
environment between 0 and 10 per cent, what accounts for the missing variation? It has been 
argued that it must be the non-shared environment, the experiences that one child has but his or 
her sibling does not. A new and controversial theory proposes that after genes the next largest 
determinant of how children turn out is the peer group and the child's particular role within it. 
 
In her book The Nurture Assumption Judith Harris used the results described above to claim that 
the missing 40–50 per cent of developmental influence is primarily caused by other children. The 
book has caused a storm and The Society for Research in Child Development recently voted her 
research the fifth most controversial study since 1950.

7 
 
Harris admits that in the initial stages of infancy parents do have an important influence. In the 
earliest years, infants learn a lot from their parents. They will usually acquire their first language 
from parental input, for example, but as soon as they start to mix with other children they learn 
things which override the earlier parental influences. According to Harris, ‘a child’s goal is not to 
become a successful adult … a child’s goal is to become a successful child’. 
 
Harris argues that there are four reasons why children might have evolved to be socialised by 
their peers rather than by their parents. First, younger members of human and non-human primate 
species tend to be the innovators (Rowe, 1994) and their young peers are also more ready to take 
up these new ideas than older members of society. Humans are competitive, and in such a 
situation it pays to adapt quickly to new things. Relying on parents would mean children 
benefiting less from useful innovations. Second, if children learned everything they knew from 
their parents, their skills and ideas would all be very similar to those of their parents. Having 
children learn from their peers adds to the variation of knowledge that is in the culture. Third, in 
the ancestral environment the chances that a child would have both parents for very long were 
relatively small. Such children would have been doomed if they had counted on their parents for 
education. And lastly, parents and children have different, often competing interests. What the 
parent might want them to learn is unlikely to be what’s best for them. 
 
So far, most of these evolutionary justifications for group socialisation theory amount to little 
more than speculation. The first two points do make some form of sense, but it must be 
remembered that the benefits of culture must ultimately be to the individual, not the species or 
society as a whole. The third point also contains much truth, but in the ancestral environment 
orphans would probably have suffered rather more than the absence of someone to learn from; 
they could well have starved. The final point is also true: parents and children do have competing 
interests much of the time. But children’s interests compete with those of other children as well; it 
is not as if children constitute an organised coalition against parental exploitation.
